newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Taiwan says no S.African petrochemical partner yet.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says no S.African petrochemical partner yet.

text.p: Taiwanese Vice Premier Hsu Li-teh said on Thursday that it would be up to the South African government and the private sector to find a suitable partner for its planned South African petrochemical plant.
Briefing the parliamentary trade and industry committee, Hsu said his delegation had come to South Africa with "a very concrete proposal which is a 50-50 percent partnership".
"In my country we have organised our team already and we hope that your government can come up with some partnership for us," he said.
He said the proposal for the project had been handed to the South African Department of Trade and Industry for consideration.

Given the government's aim to increase the involvement of black entrepreneurs in industry, and reduce the domination by large corporations, "maybe it is up to your government or your private sector to think about who can compose a consortium," Hsu said. "We have no bias."
He said government could also consider providing the funds needed to allow black business to participate in the consortium. Government support for strategic industries was common in Taiwan, he said.
There was some surprise in the petrochemicals sector this week when the state-owned Taiwanese media announced that Taiwan planned to invest more than US$3 billion in the plant.
Local companies said that the first they had heard of this was from agency reports picked up by South African newspapers.

Taiwan first expressed interest in the sector two years ago and some analysts speculated that the revival of the project was linked to efforts to get South Africa to continue diplomatic recognition of Taipei despite pressure from Beijing to switch alliances.
Hsu said he was concerned by the imbalance of trade between South Africa and Taiwan and aimed to increase imports from South Africa by at least 10 percent a year for the next three years.
He said that Taiwan was also keen to help South Africa with vocational training and had provided a grant of $40 million to support industrial parks in the Eastern Cape.
"We have seen the site... I think this is going to be one of the largest for industrial training in South Africa," Hsu said.
